title: The article that sticks to the tail
goal: Understand the two kinds of Swedish nouns and the ending that does the job of "the" — something you won't find in English, where "the" stands in front as a separate word.
bekal: tell *en*-ord from *ett*-ord, and know when it's safe to guess
turn *en bok* into *boken* — the article that attaches at the back
words for the home and everyday things

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Nyckeln är borta
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon. Dian is standing outside her door, emptying out her whole bag. Ahmad walks past carrying a bag of groceries.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Ahmad! I can't find the key.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Har du en nyckel i väskan?
lines.id: Do you have a key in your bag?
lines.literal: have you a key in bag-the?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Väskan är tom. Jag har bara en bok, en telefon och ett paraply.
lines.id: The bag's empty. I've only got a book, a phone and an umbrella.
lines.literal: bag-the is empty. I have only a book, a phone and an umbrella.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Ligger nyckeln på bordet i köket?
lines.id: Is the key on the table in the kitchen?
lines.literal: lies key-the on table-the in kitchen-the?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nej, jag tittar där varje dag. Bordet är tomt.
lines.id: No, I look there every day. The table's empty.
lines.literal: no, I look there every day. table-the is empty.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Och fickan? Jackan har två fickor.
lines.id: What about your pocket? Your jacket has two pockets.
lines.literal: and pocket-the? jacket-the has two pockets.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Oops. The key's in my pocket.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag vet. Huset är nytt och huvudet är trött.
lines.id: I know. The building's new and my head is tired.
lines.literal: I know. house-the is new and head-the is tired.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Kom, vi tar en fika. Kaffet är redan klart.
lines.id: Come on, let's have a fika. The coffee's already ready.
lines.literal: come, we take a fika. coffee-the is already ready.

notes: **Nyckeln = nyckel + n.** Swedish has no separate word for "the" in front of a noun. Instead it **glues** the article onto the tail: *en nyckel* (a key) → *nyckeln* (the key). English puts *the* in front; Swedish — along with all the Scandinavian languages — puts it at the back.

**There are two kinds of nouns**, and the kind decides the ending: *en*-ord get **-en**, *ett*-ord get **-et**. *en nyckel* → *nyckeln*; *ett bord* → *bordet*. The kind has nothing to do with male or female, and unfortunately nothing to do with meaning either. Only one thing is reliable: **about 75% of nouns are *en*-ord**, so if you're truly stuck, guess *en*.

**Adjectives change too.** *Väskan är tom* but *bordet är tomt*. An adjective describing an *ett*-ord takes a **-t** ending: *tom* → *tomt*, *ny* → *nytt*, *bra* → stays *bra*. This is covered properly in Unit 12, but start noticing it now: every time you see a *-t* at the end of an adjective, there's an *ett*-ord nearby.

**Ligger** means "lies, is lying". Swedish pays close attention to the **position** of things: something lying flat *ligger*, something upright *står*, something sitting *sitter*. A key on a table *ligger*; a bottle on a table *står*. Where English is happy with "is" ("the key is on the table"), Swedish usually picks one of these. Asking *var ligger…* about a town is normal too: *Var ligger Uppsala?* (Where is Uppsala?)

**Varje dag, varje vecka** — "every day, every week". *Varje* is always followed by the **indefinite** form (*dag*, not *dagen*), because "every" already does the pointing — just as English says "every day", not "every the day".

**Huvudet** (the head) is pronounced **HÜ-vü-deh** — the final *d* of the ending *-det* almost disappears in speech, and so does the *t* in *det*, *huset*, *bordet*. That's not laziness; it's standard pronunciation.

grammars.title: The four forms of every noun
body: Every Swedish noun has four forms. You've met two of them; the other two (plural) are the subject of Unit 5. You'll see this table again and again — get to know its layout now.
after: The singular definite ending has one adjustment: if the word **already ends in a vowel**, you add only one letter. *en flicka* → *flickan* (not *flickaen*); *ett äpple* → *äpplet* (not *äppleet*).

On the other hand, *en*-ord ending in **-el, -er, -en** lose their *e* as soon as the ending attaches: *en nyckel* → *nyckeln*, *en syster* → *systern*, *en cykel* → *cykeln*. This isn't a random exception — it happens so the word doesn't end up with two weak syllables in a row.

grammars.title: Guessing the gender fairly reliably
body: No rule is always right, but a few tendencies help more often than not.

head: Tends to be *en*
Examples
Tends to be *ett*
Examples
rows: en man, en lärare, en student
en hund, en katt, en fågel
ett hus, ett rum, ett kök
en flicka, en gata, en skola

after: The method that really works isn't memorizing rules but **learning every noun together with its article from the start**. Never store "bok" in your head; store "**en** bok". Every vocabulary table in this course is written that way, on purpose.

If you guess wrong, it's no disaster. Mixing up *en* and *ett* is the most common mistake foreigners make — including people who have lived in Sweden for years — and it never makes a sentence impossible to understand.

sections.title: When to use the definite form

blocks.text: Good news: the definite form is used almost exactly like English *the*. If you'd say "the" in English, you'll almost always want the ending in Swedish.

head: When…
Form
Example
rows: it's mentioned for the first time
there's only one in the speaker's world
something in general, a kind of thing

blocks.text: As in English, Swedish **has to** choose one or the other. No countable noun stands bare without *en/ett* or an ending, except for general things you don't count (*kaffe*, *vatten*, *mat*) and indefinite plurals. *Jag har bok* is wrong for the same reason "I have book" is wrong; the correct form is *jag har en bok*.

blocks.title: The "the" trap
items: Because English *the* is a separate word in front, learners are tempted to put an article in front **and** add the ending: *en nyckeln*. That's wrong — it's either *en nyckel* (a key) or *nyckeln* (the key).

Swedish often uses the definite form where English would say "my" or "your", especially with body parts and clothing: *huvudet är trött* = "my head is tired" (literally "the head"), *nyckeln ligger i fickan* = "the key is in my pocket". Dian does exactly this in the dialogue.
Real possessives (*min nyckel*, *hans nyckel*) are the subject of Unit 9. For now, just be aware that English "my" doesn't always mean a possessive word in Swedish.

sections.title: The home, and the things in it

blocks.text: Practice the first and second columns together: once you know the definite form, the noun's gender sticks in your memory at no extra cost.

**Ett fönster → fönstret**, not *fönsteret*: *ett*-ord ending in *-er* also lose their *e*, just like the *en*-ord above. The pattern holds for *ett mönster* → *mönstret*, *ett teater* → *teatern* — but not for many other words, so don't over-generalize.

blocks.title: Swedish words you already know
items: **en telefon, en dator, ett problem, en bank, ett hotell, en buss, en film, ett kort, en toalett, en adress** — through English, you can read nearly all of them without help (*ett kort* is a card, and *en dator* is a computer — think "data").

Watch out for words that **look alike but mean something else**: *en fabrik* (factory, not fabric), *en gift* (poison — while *gift* as an adjective means "married"), *rolig* (fun, funny), *bra* (good — nothing to do with underwear).
The word **semester** means **vacation**, not a university semester. A university semester is *en termin*. It's one of the traps that catches the most foreign students in Sweden.
